f.label: die Birne
f.en: pear

n.label: das Bonbon
n.en: sweet

sentences.en: The apple is red.
sentences.note: Apfel is masculine, so 'the' is der. After ist, the adjective takes no ending.

f.en: The pear is red.
f.note: Birne is feminine, so 'the' is die. After ist, the adjective takes no ending.

n.en: The sweet is red.
n.note: Bonbon is neuter, so 'the' is das. After ist, the adjective takes no ending.

sentences.en: It is John's apple.
sentences.note: Names take -s for possession, with no apostrophe: Johns Apfel.

mistake.why: German doesn't use an apostrophe here: Johns.

f.en: It is John's pear.
f.note: Names take -s for possession, with no apostrophe: Johns Birne.

mistake.why: German doesn't use an apostrophe here: Johns.

n.en: It is John's sweet.
n.note: Names take -s for possession, with no apostrophe: Johns Bonbon.

mistake.why: German doesn't use an apostrophe here: Johns.

sentences.en: I give John the apple.
sentences.note: The apple is the thing given, so it's accusative: der becomes den. John receives it (dative). With two nouns, the dative comes first.
sentences.hint: The apple is the object: accusative.

f.en: I give John the pear.
f.note: The pear is the thing given, so it's accusative: die stays die. John receives it (dative). With two nouns, the dative comes first.
f.hint: The pear is the object: accusative.

n.en: I give John the sweet.
n.note: The sweet is the thing given, so it's accusative: das stays das. John receives it (dative). With two nouns, the dative comes first.
n.hint: The sweet is the object: accusative.

sentences.en: We give him the apple.
sentences.note: ihm is 'him' in the dative, the one receiving. den Apfel is the accusative object.

f.en: We give him the pear.
f.note: ihm is 'him' in the dative, the one receiving. die Birne is the accusative object.

n.en: We give him the sweet.
n.note: ihm is 'him' in the dative, the one receiving. das Bonbon is the accusative object.

sentences.en: He gives it to John.
sentences.note: geben becomes gibt for er/sie/es. 'It' is the apple (masculine), so it's ihn. A pronoun object comes before a noun object.
sentences.hint: 'it' = der Apfel, and geben changes its vowel.

mistake.why: A pronoun object goes before a noun object: ihn John.

f.note: geben becomes gibt for er/sie/es. 'It' is the pear (feminine), so it's sie. A pronoun object comes before a noun object.
f.hint: 'it' = die Birne, and geben changes its vowel.

mistake.why: A pronoun object goes before a noun object: sie John.

n.note: geben becomes gibt for er/sie/es. 'It' is the sweet (neuter), so it's es. A pronoun object comes before a noun object.
n.hint: 'it' = das Bonbon, and geben changes its vowel.

mistake.why: A pronoun object goes before a noun object: es John.

sentences.en: She gives it to him.
sentences.note: Two pronouns: accusative (ihn, the apple) before dative (ihm, him). Other dative pronouns slot in the same way: Sie gibt ihn uns (to us), mir (to me).

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first.

f.note: Two pronouns: accusative (sie, the pear) before dative (ihm, him). Other dative pronouns slot in the same way: Sie gibt sie uns (to us), mir (to me).

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first.

n.note: Two pronouns: accusative (es, the sweet) before dative (ihm, him). Other dative pronouns slot in the same way: Sie gibt es uns (to us), mir (to me).

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first.

sentences.en: Is the apple red?
sentences.note: A yes/no question starts with the verb. No 'do' needed.

f.en: Is the pear red?

n.en: Is the sweet red?

sentences.en: The apples are red.
sentences.note: Apfel → Äpfel: the plural adds an umlaut. Every plural takes die. rot still has no ending after sind. Possessives take -e in the plural: meine Äpfel.
sentences.hint: Plural: the plural adds an umlaut.

f.en: The pears are red.
f.note: Birne → Birnen: the plural adds -n. Every plural takes die. rot still has no ending after sind. Possessives take -e in the plural: meine Birnen.

n.en: The sweets are red.
n.note: Bonbon → Bonbons: the plural adds -s. Every plural takes die. rot still has no ending after sind. Possessives take -e in the plural: meine Bonbons.

sentences.en: I must give it to him.
sentences.note: muss sits in position 2; geben goes to the very end. The two pronouns sit in between, accusative first.

mistake.why: The infinitive goes to the end of the sentence.
The infinitive goes to the end of the sentence.
The infinitive goes to the end of the sentence.

sentences.en: I want to give it to her.
sentences.note: ich will means 'I want'. Modals take a bare infinitive: no zu for English 'to'. ihr is 'to her'. With sie, the verb tells you who: sie will (she wants), sie wollen (they want).

mistake.wrong: Ich will zu ihn ihr geben.
mistake.why: Modal verbs take the infinitive without zu.

mistake.wrong: Ich will zu sie ihr geben.
mistake.why: Modal verbs take the infinitive without zu.

mistake.wrong: Ich will zu es ihr geben.
mistake.why: Modal verbs take the infinitive without zu.

sentences.en: I'm going to know tomorrow.
sentences.note: Future: werden in position 2, infinitive at the end. es is 'it' in the sense of 'the answer', not a thing, so it's neuter.

mistake.why: ich will means 'I want'. The future uses werden.

sentences.en: I can't eat the apple.
sentences.de: Ich kann den Apfel nicht essen.
sentences.note: kann in position 2, essen at the end, nicht directly before essen.
sentences.hint: nicht goes right before the infinitive.

mistake.wrong: Ich kann nicht den Apfel essen.
mistake.why: Not wrong, but it means 'not the apple (something else)'. For plain negation, nicht goes before essen.

f.en: I can't eat the pear.
f.de: Ich kann die Birne nicht essen.

mistake.wrong: Ich kann nicht die Birne essen.
mistake.why: Not wrong, but it means 'not the pear (something else)'. For plain negation, nicht goes before essen.

n.en: I can't eat the sweet.
n.de: Ich kann das Bonbon nicht essen.

mistake.wrong: Ich kann nicht das Bonbon essen.
mistake.why: Not wrong, but it means 'not the sweet (something else)'. For plain negation, nicht goes before essen.

sentences.en: I have eaten the apple.
sentences.note: Perfekt: haben in position 2, participle gegessen at the end. This is also how German says 'I ate the apple' in conversation.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

f.en: I have eaten the pear.
f.note: Perfekt: haben in position 2, participle gegessen at the end. This is also how German says 'I ate the pear' in conversation.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

n.en: I have eaten the sweet.
n.note: Perfekt: haben in position 2, participle gegessen at the end. This is also how German says 'I ate the sweet' in conversation.

mistake.why: The participle goes to the end.

sentences.en: This is an apple.
sentences.note: Apfel is masculine (der), so the indefinite article in the nominative is ein. Das here means 'this' and doesn't change with gender.

f.en: This is a pear.
f.note: Birne is feminine (die), so the indefinite article in the nominative is eine. Das here means 'this' and doesn't change with gender.

n.en: This is a sweet.
n.note: Bonbon is neuter (das), so the indefinite article in the nominative is ein. Das here means 'this' and doesn't change with gender.

sentences.en: I give John his apple.
sentences.note: The apple is the accusative object, so sein takes -en: seinen, like einen. For a woman's things, 'her' is ihr with the same endings: Ich gebe Anna ihren Apfel.
sentences.hint: sein takes the same ending as ein would.

f.en: I give John his pear.
f.note: The pear is the accusative object, so sein takes -e: seine, like eine. For a woman's things, 'her' is ihr with the same endings: Ich gebe Anna ihre Birne.

n.en: I give John his sweet.
n.note: The sweet is the accusative object, so sein takes no ending: sein, like ein. For a woman's things, 'her' is ihr with the same endings: Ich gebe Anna ihr Bonbon.

sentences.en: But I do not want the apple either.
sentences.de: Aber ich will den Apfel auch nicht.
sentences.note: aber doesn't take a slot, so the order after it is normal V2. To negate the whole statement, nicht goes after the definite object (Sie will den Apfel nicht); auch nicht = 'not either'.

f.en: But I do not want the pear either.
f.de: Aber ich will die Birne auch nicht.
f.note: aber doesn't take a slot, so the order after it is normal V2. To negate the whole statement, nicht goes after the definite object (Sie will die Birne nicht); auch nicht = 'not either'.

n.en: But I do not want the sweet either.
n.de: Aber ich will das Bonbon auch nicht.
n.note: aber doesn't take a slot, so the order after it is normal V2. To negate the whole statement, nicht goes after the definite object (Sie will das Bonbon nicht); auch nicht = 'not either'.

sentences.en: It's not mine.
sentences.note: 'It' is er because it refers to der Apfel. The standalone possessive shows the gender too: meiner.

mistake.why: Standing alone, the possessive needs a gender ending: meiner.

f.note: 'It' is sie because it refers to die Birne. The standalone possessive shows the gender too: meine.

mistake.why: Standing alone, the possessive needs a gender ending: meine.

n.note: 'It' is es because it refers to das Bonbon. The standalone possessive shows the gender too: meins.

mistake.why: Standing alone, the possessive needs a gender ending: meins.

sentences.en: I will not take the red apple.
sentences.de: Ich werde den roten Apfel nicht nehmen.
sentences.note: werden + infinitive for the future. After den, the adjective takes the weak ending -en: den roten Apfel. Add a receiver and it goes before the apple: Ich werde dir den roten Apfel geben.

f.en: I will not take the red pear.
f.de: Ich werde die rote Birne nicht nehmen.
f.note: werden + infinitive for the future. After die, the adjective takes the weak ending -e: die rote Birne. Add a receiver and it goes before the pear: Ich werde dir die rote Birne geben.

n.en: I will not take the red sweet.
n.de: Ich werde das rote Bonbon nicht nehmen.
n.note: werden + infinitive for the future. After das, the adjective takes the weak ending -e: das rote Bonbon. Add a receiver and it goes before the sweet: Ich werde dir das rote Bonbon geben.

sentences.en: Do you want an apple?
sentences.note: Verb first for a yes/no question. möchtest ('would you like') is the polite everyday way to offer something.

f.en: Do you want a pear?

n.en: Do you want a sweet?

sentences.en: Which one do you want?
sentences.note: welch- declines like der. It stands for a masculine accusative (den Apfel), so it's welchen.

f.note: welch- declines like der. It stands for a feminine accusative (die Birne), so it's welche.

n.note: welch- declines like der. It stands for a neuter accusative (das Bonbon), so it's welches.

sentences.en: It was John's apple.
sentences.note: war is the simple past of sein. Spoken German uses war, not ist gewesen, for everyday 'was'.

f.en: It was John's pear.

n.en: It was John's sweet.

sentences.en: But he said he doesn't want it anymore.
sentences.de: Aber er hat gesagt, dass er ihn nicht mehr will.
sentences.note: The main clause is Perfekt (hat … gesagt). dass sends will to the end of its clause.
sentences.hint: dass sends the verb to the end.

mistake.wrong: …, dass er will ihn nicht mehr.
mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes last.

f.de: Aber er hat gesagt, dass er sie nicht mehr will.

mistake.wrong: …, dass er will sie nicht mehr.
mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes last.

n.de: Aber er hat gesagt, dass er es nicht mehr will.

mistake.wrong: …, dass er will es nicht mehr.
mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes last.

sentences.en: So now it is yours.
sentences.note: jetzt takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject er follows it. gehören takes a dative: 'belongs to you'.
sentences.hint: Start with jetzt; the verb still comes second.

mistake.why: The verb must be second: Jetzt gehört er.

f.note: jetzt takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject sie follows it. gehören takes a dative: 'belongs to you'.

mistake.why: The verb must be second: Jetzt gehört sie.

n.note: jetzt takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject es follows it. gehören takes a dative: 'belongs to you'.

mistake.why: The verb must be second: Jetzt gehört es.

sentences.en: You should eat it.
sentences.note: solltest (subjunctive of sollen) gives advice: 'you should'. du sollst is closer to 'you're supposed to'.

sentences.en: Why didn't you eat it?
sentences.de: Warum hast du ihn nicht gegessen?
sentences.note: warum first, hast second, gegessen last. nicht comes right before the participle. The yes/no version just starts with the verb: Hast du den Apfel gegessen?

f.de: Warum hast du sie nicht gegessen?
f.note: warum first, hast second, gegessen last. nicht comes right before the participle. The yes/no version just starts with the verb: Hast du die Birne gegessen?

n.de: Warum hast du es nicht gegessen?
n.note: warum first, hast second, gegessen last. nicht comes right before the participle. The yes/no version just starts with the verb: Hast du das Bonbon gegessen?

sentences.en: If you ate it, you would be happy.
sentences.de: Wenn du ihn essen würdest, wärst du glücklich.
sentences.note: The wenn-clause puts würdest last. The whole clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb: wärst du.
sentences.hint: After the wenn-clause, the verb comes next.

f.de: Wenn du sie essen würdest, wärst du glücklich.

n.de: Wenn du es essen würdest, wärst du glücklich.

sentences.en: They will eat all of the apples.
sentences.note: alle goes straight before the noun. No word for 'of'.

f.en: They will eat all of the pears.

n.en: They will eat all of the sweets.

sentences.en: And there are a lot of apples to eat.
sentences.de: Und es gibt viele Äpfel zu essen.
sentences.note: 'There are' is es gibt, even for plurals. The object is accusative. 'to eat' is zu essen.

f.en: And there are a lot of pears to eat.
f.de: Und es gibt viele Birnen zu essen.

n.en: And there are a lot of sweets to eat.
n.de: Und es gibt viele Bonbons zu essen.

sentences.en: Most of them are red.
sentences.de: Die meisten von ihnen sind rot.
sentences.note: die meisten = 'most'. von takes the dative: ihnen. Swap in other amounts: einige von ihnen (some), ein paar von ihnen (a few; ein Paar with a capital P is 'a pair').

sentences.en: And none of the apples are blue.
sentences.de: Und keiner der Äpfel ist blau.
sentences.note: der Äpfel is genitive plural ('of the apples'). keiner is singular, so the verb is ist. 'One of the apples' works the same way: einer der Äpfel.

f.en: And none of the pears are blue.
f.de: Und keine der Birnen ist blau.
f.note: der Birnen is genitive plural ('of the pears'). keine is singular, so the verb is ist. 'One of the pears' works the same way: eine der Birnen.

n.en: And none of the sweets are blue.
n.de: Und keins der Bonbons ist blau.
n.note: der Bonbons is genitive plural ('of the sweets'). keins is singular, so the verb is ist. 'One of the sweets' works the same way: eins der Bonbons.

sentences.en: These are beautiful, big, red apples.
sentences.de: Das sind schöne, große, rote Äpfel.
sentences.note: No article before a plural noun, so every adjective takes the strong ending -e (also: Kleine Äpfel sind auch gut). Das sind = 'these are'.
sentences.hint: No article, so each adjective ends in -e.

f.en: These are beautiful, big, red pears.
f.de: Das sind schöne, große, rote Birnen.
f.note: No article before a plural noun, so every adjective takes the strong ending -e (also: Kleine Birnen sind auch gut). Das sind = 'these are'.

n.en: These are beautiful, big, red sweets.
n.de: Das sind schöne, große, rote Bonbons.
n.note: No article before a plural noun, so every adjective takes the strong ending -e (also: Kleine Bonbons sind auch gut). Das sind = 'these are'.

sentences.en: You can have as many as you want.
sentences.de: Du kannst so viele haben, wie du willst.
sentences.note: so viele … wie = 'as many as'. The wie-clause sends willst to the end.
sentences.hint: 'as many as' is so viele wie.

sentences.en: Because I have enough for everyone.
sentences.de: Weil ich genug für alle habe.
sentences.note: weil sends habe to the end. für takes the accusative. On its own like this, it's a spoken answer to 'Warum?'.
sentences.hint: weil sends the verb to the end.

mistake.wrong: Weil ich habe genug für alle.
mistake.why: Common in casual speech, but standard German puts the verb last after weil.

sentences.en: Almost everyone likes apples.
sentences.note: jeder is singular, so the verb is mag (from mögen, 'to like').

f.en: Almost everyone likes pears.

n.en: Almost everyone likes sweets.

sentences.en: The biggest ones are the best.
sentences.note: Superlatives used as nouns: die größten, die besten. groß adds an umlaut; gut is irregular (besser, best-).

sentences.en: But the big apples are better.
sentences.de: Aber die großen Äpfel sind besser.
sentences.note: After die (plural), the adjective takes -en: die großen Äpfel. gut → besser.
sentences.hint: After die (plural), the adjective ends in -en.

f.en: But the big pears are better.
f.de: Aber die großen Birnen sind besser.
f.note: After die (plural), the adjective takes -en: die großen Birnen. gut → besser.

n.en: But the big sweets are better.
n.de: Aber die großen Bonbons sind besser.
n.note: After die (plural), the adjective takes -en: die großen Bonbons. gut → besser.

sentences.en: The child eats the apple.
sentences.note: Kind is neuter (das Kind), even though a child is a person: grammatical gender doesn't follow meaning. essen changes its vowel like geben: er isst.

f.en: The child eats the pear.

n.en: The child eats the sweet.

sentences.en: I give the child the apple.
sentences.de: Ich gebe dem Kind den Apfel.
sentences.note: The child receives it: neuter dative, das Kind → dem Kind. The apple is the thing given: den Apfel.

mistake.wrong: Ich gebe der Kind den Apfel.
mistake.why: Kind is neuter, so the dative is dem.

f.en: I give the child the pear.
f.de: Ich gebe dem Kind die Birne.
f.note: The child receives it: neuter dative, das Kind → dem Kind. The pear is the thing given: die Birne.

mistake.wrong: Ich gebe der Kind die Birne.
mistake.why: Kind is neuter, so the dative is dem.

n.en: I give the child the sweet.
n.de: Ich gebe dem Kind das Bonbon.
n.note: The child receives it: neuter dative, das Kind → dem Kind. The sweet is the thing given: das Bonbon.

mistake.wrong: Ich gebe der Kind das Bonbon.
mistake.why: Kind is neuter, so the dative is dem.

sentences.en: I don't have an apple.
sentences.note: To negate a noun with ein, use kein, with the same ending: einen → keinen.

mistake.why: Use kein to negate a noun with ein: keinen Apfel.

f.en: I don't have a pear.
f.note: To negate a noun with ein, use kein, with the same ending: eine → keine.

mistake.why: Use kein to negate a noun with ein: keine Birne.

n.en: I don't have a sweet.
n.note: To negate a noun with ein, use kein, with the same ending: ein → kein.

mistake.why: Use kein to negate a noun with ein: kein Bonbon.

sentences.en: Give me the apple!
sentences.note: du-command: take du gibst, drop du and -st → Gib!

f.en: Give me the pear!

n.en: Give me the sweet!

sentences.en: Would you like an apple? (formal)
sentences.note: Formal 'you' is Sie, always capitalised, with the same verb form as 'they': möchten.
sentences.hint: Formal Sie uses the 'they' verb form.

f.en: Would you like a pear? (formal)

n.en: Would you like a sweet? (formal)

sentences.en: I put the apple on the table.
sentences.de: Ich lege den Apfel auf den Tisch.
sentences.note: Movement to a place (where to?) → auf + accusative: auf den Tisch.

mistake.wrong: Ich lege den Apfel auf dem Tisch.
mistake.why: legen is movement to a place, so auf takes the accusative: den Tisch.

f.en: I put the pear on the table.
f.de: Ich lege die Birne auf den Tisch.

mistake.wrong: Ich lege die Birne auf dem Tisch.
mistake.why: legen is movement to a place, so auf takes the accusative: den Tisch.

n.en: I put the sweet on the table.
n.de: Ich lege das Bonbon auf den Tisch.

mistake.wrong: Ich lege das Bonbon auf dem Tisch.
mistake.why: legen is movement to a place, so auf takes the accusative: den Tisch.

sentences.en: The apple is lying on the table.
sentences.de: Der Apfel liegt auf dem Tisch.
sentences.note: Location (where?) → auf + dative: auf dem Tisch. Compare legen (put) and liegen (lie).

f.en: The pear is lying on the table.
f.de: Die Birne liegt auf dem Tisch.

n.en: The sweet is lying on the table.
n.de: Das Bonbon liegt auf dem Tisch.

sentences.en: The apple fell off the table.
sentences.de: Der Apfel ist vom Tisch gefallen.
sentences.note: fallen is movement, so its Perfekt uses sein. vom = von dem (von takes the dative).

mistake.wrong: Der Apfel hat vom Tisch gefallen.
mistake.why: Verbs of movement form the Perfekt with sein.

f.en: The pear fell off the table.
f.de: Die Birne ist vom Tisch gefallen.

mistake.wrong: Die Birne hat vom Tisch gefallen.
mistake.why: Verbs of movement form the Perfekt with sein.

n.en: The sweet fell off the table.
n.de: Das Bonbon ist vom Tisch gefallen.

mistake.wrong: Das Bonbon hat vom Tisch gefallen.
mistake.why: Verbs of movement form the Perfekt with sein.

sentences.en: I'll bring an apple along tomorrow.
sentences.de: Ich bringe morgen einen Apfel mit.
sentences.note: mitbringen splits: bringe in position 2, mit at the end. Present tense + morgen is the usual way to talk about the future.

mistake.why: The prefix separates and goes to the end: bringe … mit.

f.en: I'll bring a pear along tomorrow.
f.de: Ich bringe morgen eine Birne mit.

mistake.why: The prefix separates and goes to the end: bringe … mit.

n.en: I'll bring a sweet along tomorrow.
n.de: Ich bringe morgen ein Bonbon mit.

mistake.why: The prefix separates and goes to the end: bringe … mit.

sentences.en: The apple that I bought is red.
sentences.de: Der Apfel, den ich gekauft habe, ist rot.
sentences.note: den is masculine (der Apfel) and accusative (I bought it). habe goes to the end of the relative clause.
sentences.hint: 'that' takes the gender of Apfel: den.

f.en: The pear that I bought is red.
f.de: Die Birne, die ich gekauft habe, ist rot.
f.note: die is feminine (die Birne) and accusative (I bought it). habe goes to the end of the relative clause.
f.hint: 'that' takes the gender of Birne: die.

n.en: The sweet that I bought is red.
n.de: Das Bonbon, das ich gekauft habe, ist rot.
n.note: das is neuter (das Bonbon) and accusative (I bought it). habe goes to the end of the relative clause.
n.hint: 'that' takes the gender of Bonbon: das.

sentences.en: I'm looking forward to the apple.
sentences.de: Ich freue mich auf den Apfel.
sentences.note: sich freuen auf + accusative = 'to look forward to'. The reflexive mich matches ich.

mistake.why: sich freuen is reflexive: Ich freue mich.

f.en: I'm looking forward to the pear.
f.de: Ich freue mich auf die Birne.

mistake.why: sich freuen is reflexive: Ich freue mich.

n.en: I'm looking forward to the sweet.
n.de: Ich freue mich auf das Bonbon.

mistake.why: sich freuen is reflexive: Ich freue mich.

sentences.en: I eat an apple in the kitchen every day.
sentences.de: Ich esse jeden Tag in der Küche einen Apfel.
sentences.note: Time (jeden Tag) before place (in der Küche). The new object (einen Apfel) comes late. in + dative for location.

f.en: I eat a pear in the kitchen every day.
f.de: Ich esse jeden Tag in der Küche eine Birne.
f.note: Time (jeden Tag) before place (in der Küche). The new object (eine Birne) comes late. in + dative for location.

n.en: I eat a sweet in the kitchen every day.
n.de: Ich esse jeden Tag in der Küche ein Bonbon.
n.note: Time (jeden Tag) before place (in der Küche). The new object (ein Bonbon) comes late. in + dative for location.

sentences.en: I give Anna her apple.
sentences.note: Anna is a woman, so 'her' is ihr, which takes the same endings as ein: ihren, like einen. Compare John's: Ich gebe John seinen Apfel. Watch out: ihr also means 'to her', 'you' (plural) and, as Ihr, the formal 'your'.

mistake.why: sein means 'his'. For something of Anna's, use ihr: ihren Apfel.

f.en: I give Anna her pear.
f.note: Anna is a woman, so 'her' is ihr, which takes the same endings as ein: ihre, like eine. Compare John's: Ich gebe John seine Birne. Watch out: ihr also means 'to her', 'you' (plural) and, as Ihr, the formal 'your'.

mistake.why: sein means 'his'. For something of Anna's, use ihr: ihre Birne.

n.en: I give Anna her sweet.
n.note: Anna is a woman, so 'her' is ihr, which takes the same endings as ein: ihr, like ein. Compare John's: Ich gebe John sein Bonbon. Watch out: ihr also means 'to her', 'you' (plural) and, as Ihr, the formal 'your'.

mistake.why: sein means 'his'. For something of Anna's, use ihr: ihr Bonbon.

sentences.en: She gave it to her.
sentences.note: Three pronouns in one sentence: sie (she, the one giving), ihn (it: the apple, accusative) and ihr (to her: Anna, dative). Accusative before dative. Perfekt: hat in position 2, gegeben at the end.

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: ihn ihr.

f.note: Three pronouns in one sentence: sie (she, the one giving), sie (it: the pear, accusative) and ihr (to her: Anna, dative). Accusative before dative. Perfekt: hat in position 2, gegeben at the end.

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: sie ihr.

n.note: Three pronouns in one sentence: sie (she, the one giving), es (it: the sweet, accusative) and ihr (to her: Anna, dative). Accusative before dative. Perfekt: hat in position 2, gegeben at the end.

mistake.why: With two pronouns, the accusative comes first: es ihr.

sentences.en: The apple is being eaten by John.
sentences.de: Der Apfel wird von John gegessen.
sentences.note: Passive: werden in position 2, the participle at the end. The apple is now the subject (nominative: der Apfel); whoever does it comes in with von + dative. The active version: John isst den Apfel.

mistake.wrong: Der Apfel ist von John gegessen.
mistake.why: ist + participle describes the finished state. For the action, with who does it, use wird.

f.en: The pear is being eaten by John.
f.de: Die Birne wird von John gegessen.
f.note: Passive: werden in position 2, the participle at the end. The pear is now the subject (nominative: die Birne); whoever does it comes in with von + dative. The active version: John isst die Birne.

mistake.wrong: Die Birne ist von John gegessen.
mistake.why: ist + participle describes the finished state. For the action, with who does it, use wird.

n.en: The sweet is being eaten by John.
n.de: Das Bonbon wird von John gegessen.
n.note: Passive: werden in position 2, the participle at the end. The sweet is now the subject (nominative: das Bonbon); whoever does it comes in with von + dative. The active version: John isst das Bonbon.

mistake.wrong: Das Bonbon ist von John gegessen.
mistake.why: ist + participle describes the finished state. For the action, with who does it, use wird.

sentences.en: The apple must be eaten.
sentences.note: Passive with a modal: the modal in position 2, then participle + werden at the very end. Compare the active: Man muss den Apfel essen.

mistake.why: The participle comes first: gegessen werden.

f.en: The pear must be eaten.
f.note: Passive with a modal: the modal in position 2, then participle + werden at the very end. Compare the active: Man muss die Birne essen.

mistake.why: The participle comes first: gegessen werden.

n.en: The sweet must be eaten.
n.note: Passive with a modal: the modal in position 2, then participle + werden at the very end. Compare the active: Man muss das Bonbon essen.

mistake.why: The participle comes first: gegessen werden.

sentences.en: I let John eat the apple.
sentences.de: Ich lasse John den Apfel essen.
sentences.note: lassen works like a modal: lassen in position 2, a bare infinitive at the end. It means 'let' or 'have something done': Ich lasse den Apfel waschen (I have the apple washed).
sentences.hint: lassen + infinitive at the end, no zu.

mistake.wrong: Ich lasse John den Apfel zu essen.
mistake.why: lassen takes the infinitive without zu, like a modal.

f.en: I let John eat the pear.
f.de: Ich lasse John die Birne essen.
f.note: lassen works like a modal: lassen in position 2, a bare infinitive at the end. It means 'let' or 'have something done': Ich lasse die Birne waschen (I have the pear washed).

mistake.wrong: Ich lasse John die Birne zu essen.
mistake.why: lassen takes the infinitive without zu, like a modal.

n.en: I let John eat the sweet.
n.de: Ich lasse John das Bonbon essen.
n.note: lassen works like a modal: lassen in position 2, a bare infinitive at the end. It means 'let' or 'have something done': Ich lasse das Bonbon waschen (I have the sweet washed).

mistake.wrong: Ich lasse John das Bonbon zu essen.
mistake.why: lassen takes the infinitive without zu, like a modal.

sentences.en: If I had eaten the apple, I would have been happy.
sentences.de: Wenn ich den Apfel gegessen hätte, wäre ich glücklich gewesen.
sentences.note: Past conditional: hätte or wäre + participle, for things that didn't happen. Compare the present version: Wenn du ihn essen würdest, wärst du glücklich. The wenn-clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ich den Apfel gegessen hätte, ich wäre glücklich gewesen.
mistake.why: The wenn-clause takes position 1, so the verb comes next: wäre ich.

f.en: If I had eaten the pear, I would have been happy.
f.de: Wenn ich die Birne gegessen hätte, wäre ich glücklich gewesen.
f.note: Past conditional: hätte or wäre + participle, for things that didn't happen. Compare the present version: Wenn du sie essen würdest, wärst du glücklich. The wenn-clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ich die Birne gegessen hätte, ich wäre glücklich gewesen.
mistake.why: The wenn-clause takes position 1, so the verb comes next: wäre ich.

n.en: If I had eaten the sweet, I would have been happy.
n.de: Wenn ich das Bonbon gegessen hätte, wäre ich glücklich gewesen.
n.note: Past conditional: hätte or wäre + participle, for things that didn't happen. Compare the present version: Wenn du es essen würdest, wärst du glücklich. The wenn-clause fills position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ich das Bonbon gegessen hätte, ich wäre glücklich gewesen.
mistake.why: The wenn-clause takes position 1, so the verb comes next: wäre ich.

sentences.en: He says he doesn't want the apple.
sentences.de: Er sagt, er wolle den Apfel nicht.
sentences.note: Reported speech (Konjunktiv I): er will becomes er wolle. It marks the words as his, not the speaker's claim, which is why news reports use it. In conversation, people usually say: Er sagt, dass er den Apfel nicht will.

f.en: He says he doesn't want the pear.
f.de: Er sagt, er wolle die Birne nicht.
f.note: Reported speech (Konjunktiv I): er will becomes er wolle. It marks the words as his, not the speaker's claim, which is why news reports use it. In conversation, people usually say: Er sagt, dass er die Birne nicht will.

n.en: He says he doesn't want the sweet.
n.de: Er sagt, er wolle das Bonbon nicht.
n.note: Reported speech (Konjunktiv I): er will becomes er wolle. It marks the words as his, not the speaker's claim, which is why news reports use it. In conversation, people usually say: Er sagt, dass er das Bonbon nicht will.

sentences.en: He must have eaten the apple.
sentences.de: Er muss den Apfel gegessen haben.
sentences.note: A modal + participle + haben makes a guess about the past: 'must have …'. With können it's 'may have': Er kann ihn gegessen haben.

mistake.wrong: Er muss den Apfel haben gegessen.
mistake.why: The participle comes before haben: gegessen haben.

f.en: He must have eaten the pear.
f.de: Er muss die Birne gegessen haben.
f.note: A modal + participle + haben makes a guess about the past: 'must have …'. With können it's 'may have': Er kann sie gegessen haben.

mistake.wrong: Er muss die Birne haben gegessen.
mistake.why: The participle comes before haben: gegessen haben.

n.en: He must have eaten the sweet.
n.de: Er muss das Bonbon gegessen haben.
n.note: A modal + participle + haben makes a guess about the past: 'must have …'. With können it's 'may have': Er kann es gegessen haben.

mistake.wrong: Er muss das Bonbon haben gegessen.
mistake.why: The participle comes before haben: gegessen haben.

sentences.en: I wasn't able to eat the apple.
sentences.de: Ich habe den Apfel nicht essen können.
sentences.note: The Perfekt of a modal used with another verb ends in two infinitives (essen können), not gekonnt. In speech the simple past is more common: Ich konnte den Apfel nicht essen.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe den Apfel nicht essen gekonnt.
mistake.why: With another verb, the modal stays an infinitive: essen können.

f.en: I wasn't able to eat the pear.
f.de: Ich habe die Birne nicht essen können.
f.note: The Perfekt of a modal used with another verb ends in two infinitives (essen können), not gekonnt. In speech the simple past is more common: Ich konnte die Birne nicht essen.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe die Birne nicht essen gekonnt.
mistake.why: With another verb, the modal stays an infinitive: essen können.

n.en: I wasn't able to eat the sweet.
n.de: Ich habe das Bonbon nicht essen können.
n.note: The Perfekt of a modal used with another verb ends in two infinitives (essen können), not gekonnt. In speech the simple past is more common: Ich konnte das Bonbon nicht essen.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe das Bonbon nicht essen gekonnt.
mistake.why: With another verb, the modal stays an infinitive: essen können.

sentences.en: They are arguing because of the apple.
sentences.note: wegen takes the genitive: des Apfels. Masculine and neuter nouns add -s in the genitive; feminine nouns don't change. In everyday speech you'll also hear wegen + dative: wegen dem Apfel.

f.en: They are arguing because of the pear.
f.note: wegen takes the genitive: der Birne. Masculine and neuter nouns add -s in the genitive; feminine nouns don't change. In everyday speech you'll also hear wegen + dative: wegen der Birne.

n.en: They are arguing because of the sweet.
n.note: wegen takes the genitive: des Bonbons. Masculine and neuter nouns add -s in the genitive; feminine nouns don't change. In everyday speech you'll also hear wegen + dative: wegen dem Bonbon.

sentences.en: The bigger the apple, the better it tastes.
sentences.de: Je größer der Apfel ist, desto besser schmeckt er.
sentences.note: je + comparative opens a clause with the verb at the end (ist). desto + comparative starts the main clause and the verb follows straight away: desto besser schmeckt er.
sentences.hint: je … verb last; desto … verb next.

mistake.wrong: Je größer der Apfel ist, desto besser er schmeckt.
mistake.why: After desto + comparative, the verb comes next: desto besser schmeckt er.

f.en: The bigger the pear, the better it tastes.
f.de: Je größer die Birne ist, desto besser schmeckt sie.
f.note: je + comparative opens a clause with the verb at the end (ist). desto + comparative starts the main clause and the verb follows straight away: desto besser schmeckt sie.

mistake.wrong: Je größer die Birne ist, desto besser sie schmeckt.
mistake.why: After desto + comparative, the verb comes next: desto besser schmeckt sie.

n.en: The bigger the sweet, the better it tastes.
n.de: Je größer das Bonbon ist, desto besser schmeckt es.
n.note: je + comparative opens a clause with the verb at the end (ist). desto + comparative starts the main clause and the verb follows straight away: desto besser schmeckt es.

mistake.wrong: Je größer das Bonbon ist, desto besser es schmeckt.
mistake.why: After desto + comparative, the verb comes next: desto besser schmeckt es.

sentences.en: The apple that fell off the table is red.
sentences.de: Der vom Tisch gefallene Apfel ist rot.
sentences.note: An extended participle phrase: everything between der and Apfel describes the apple, like a relative clause folded in front of the noun. The same meaning, spoken style: Der Apfel, der vom Tisch gefallen ist, ist rot. Typical of written German.
sentences.hint: Everything between the article and the noun describes it.

f.en: The pear that fell off the table is red.
f.de: Die vom Tisch gefallene Birne ist rot.
f.note: An extended participle phrase: everything between die and Birne describes the pear, like a relative clause folded in front of the noun. The same meaning, spoken style: Die Birne, die vom Tisch gefallen ist, ist rot. Typical of written German.

n.en: The sweet that fell off the table is red.
n.de: Das vom Tisch gefallene Bonbon ist rot.
n.note: An extended participle phrase: everything between das and Bonbon describes the sweet, like a relative clause folded in front of the noun. The same meaning, spoken style: Das Bonbon, das vom Tisch gefallen ist, ist rot. Typical of written German.
